Agentic LLM systems have moved from linear prompt chains to graph-based workflows and, more recently, code-executing harnesses. items.title: MCP-warden local credential broker so AI agents never see your secrets
items.story_key: story|title:mcp warden local credential broker so ai agents never see your secrets
items.content_excerpt: Local-first credential broker for MCP. AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex…) call APIs, SSH and databases through scoped presets; secrets stay in your OS keychain and never enter the agent's context. A local-first credential broker for the Model Context Protocol — lets any AI coding agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Cline, Codex, Continue, Zed) take real actions without ever seeing your secrets. The agent calls high-level tools ( proxy_http ); mcp-warden injects the secret server-side, executes the action, and returns only the result. Your context window stays clean. A leaked transcript leaks nothing useful. Pre-built binaries for macOS (x86_64, aarch64) and Linux (x86_64), each with a SHA-256 checksum, are attached to every GitHub release . The preset auto-approves only GET /user/repos ; any other path is refused before the token is touched. To let the agent read more, widen the allow-list (e.g. --allowed-paths '/user/repos,/repos/OWNER/[^/]+' ) and prefer a fine-grained PAT limited to specific repos. Patterns match the whole path, as exact strings or regexes anchored as ^(?:…)$ , never as prefixes; [^/]+ is safer than .* for one segment. They see the percent-decoded path, so %2F is a separator: a GitLab-style id like /projects/group%2Fproject needs /projects/[^/]+/[^/]+ . An HTTP preset with no allowed_paths allows every path under base_url — preset add and doctor warn about it, and the built-in github-read / gitea-read / stripe-read templates ship with approval = "prompt" for that reason. Wire mcp-warden into your agent — see docs/claude-code-setup.md or docs/cursor-setup.md . In your agent: ask "list my GitHub repos via mcp-warden". Watch the agent call list_presets , then proxy_http — and watch your PAT stay out of the prompt. For Claude Code there is a plugin that bundles the MCP server config, a skill that teaches Claude to use mcp-warden correctly (discover presets first, never ask for tokens, respect approvals, treat get_secret_for_env as a last resort) and a guided /mcp-warden:setup command. Install the binary first, then in Claude Code: Restart Claude Code and run /mcp-warden:setup . If you previously added the server with claude mcp add , remove that entry so it isn't registered twice. Details: plugins/mcp-warden/ . Other MCP clients: see docs/claude-code-setup.md and docs/cursor-setup.md for manual setup. mcp-warden 's threat model and security invariants live in docs/threat-model.md . At a glance: mcp-warden stays fully functional for free

items.title: Keeping API keys out of our AI agent's sandbox, and what that doesn't solve
items.story_key: story|title:keeping api keys out of our ai agent s sandbox and what that doesn t solve
items.content_excerpt: Doozy runs tasks against our customers' databases, Stripe and GitHub from a Slack thread. Here's how the agent does that without ever holding a key, and the risks a missing key doesn't remove. Doozy is an AI agent people mention in Slack. Someone writes "@Doozy why was Acme charged twice?" in a support thread, and it goes and checks: it queries the database , reads Stripe , looks at the code in GitHub , and posts what it found back in the thread. So the first question every engineer asks me is about AI agent security, and it's the right one: you're giving an LLM production credentials? This is the long answer. Most of it is deliberately boring. The interesting part is what's left over once the keys are gone. The agent never holds an API key. Each task runs in a fresh sandbox that holds only a signed, short-lived job token. A credential proxy outside the sandbox checks that token, decides whether the tool is allowed, and adds the real key to that one call. Database queries run read-only, with a timeout and a row cap. That stops keys leaking. It doesn't stop prompt injection misusing the tools you've switched on, so those are the controls that matter most. Every task runs in its own sandbox, a small VM that exists for that one job and is thrown away after. Nothing in it is a credential for your systems. No API keys, no database password, no model provider key, no GitHub token. When the agent needs something outside, the call leaves the sandbox and goes to a gateway we run. The gateway decides whether the call is allowed, attaches the right credential, forwards it, and passes the response back. The agent sees results. It never sees the secret that produced them. None of this is new. A credential proxy, a service that injects keys into requests so the caller never sees them, is an old pattern, the one you'd draw on a whiteboard in five minutes. That's the point. When the thing on the other side of the boundary is a language model that will read anything it can reach, I want the boundary to be the most boring part of the system. It matters because prompt injection isn't solved, and I don't expect it to be soon. A support ticket, a web page, a PDF someone drops in the thread: any of it can carry instructions. If one gets through, the agent can misuse the tools it has. What it can't do is print a key, write it to a file or send it somewhere, because there isn't one to find. The sandbox isn't empty. It holds a job token, and every call it makes carries it. If you'

items.title: RFC AI Tooling: 40x fewer tokens while reading the RFC corpus
items.story_key: story|title:rfc ai tooling 40x fewer tokens while reading the rfc corpus
items.content_excerpt: Let AI agents read the RFC corpus with 40x fewer tokens, and flag obsoleted specs. Two ways to give an AI agent the IETF RFC corpus: a skill and an MCP server. Both run the same stdlib-only Python core, so they find, read and flag documents identically. No RFC text ships with either; documents come from the RFC Editor on demand. The median saving is 41x, the figure behind "40x fewer tokens". Tokens are approximated as bytes divided by 4, measured from rfc.py 0.5.0 output. assets/charts/context_sizes.json has the raw measurements. Agents cite dead specifications with confidence. RFC 2616 has been obsolete since 2014, and it's still the first thing most models reach for on HTTP. Every result here carries the RFC index's obsolescence field, so the agent follows the replacement before it quotes anything. Add this to your client's MCP configuration. uvx fetches mcp-server-rfc from PyPI on first run. I've tested it end to end in Claude Desktop on Linux. macOS and Windows should work, but I haven't checked them. docs/desktop-verification.md shows how to tell whether Desktop really called the tools. Then add https://<your-app>/mcp as a custom connector in claude.ai, which needs a Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise plan. The agent runs the same loop you can run yourself: search, check obsolescence, list sections, read one. Title search works with no setup. To search the text of every RFC, download the section index once. For the skill, where <skills-dir> is where it was installed, like ~/.claude/skills : The index is a SQLite file holding every RFC, compressed, and an FTS5 index over each section. A search returns sections ranked by BM25, with the number to read next: Reads come from the index too, so nothing is fetched from the RFC Editor after that. On the retrieval eval it finds the answering section in its top 10 for more than half of the held-out questions; ripgrep over the corpus finds it for none. Without the index, --fulltext falls back to rg or grep over a synced mirror of the corpus as plain files, which is also what --regex needs: Neither starts on its own, and the skill tells agents not to run them unasked. rfc index build makes the index from a synced mirror, in about two and a half minutes. core/rfc.py is the only implementation. The skill and the MCP server each carry an identical copy, and CI fails if one drifts. items.title: Evaluating DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 for loss of control and harmful manipulation risks
items.summary: As frontier language models grow increasingly capable and autonomous, independent third-party evaluations are critical for characterizing their systemic safety risks. While closed-source releases are routinely accompanied by comprehensive system cards, open-weight models receive less scrutiny regarding frontier risks. To address this gap, we present an independent safety evaluation of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017, the latest version of V4.1 Flash that departs from V4 with a new architecture, scaled-up training, and strong agentic capabilities. Drawing on the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, we evaluate the model across 34 benchmarks, including 5 in-house suites, spanning evaluation integrity, loss of control, and harmful manipulation. Conforming to the AEF-1 standard, we compare V4.1 Flash-1017 against V4.1 Flash, earlier DeepSeek V4 models, and leading closed-source systems (GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Gemini 3.8 Flash). Overall, V4.1 Flash-1017 shows substantial safety improvements over the V4 generation and approaches or matches leading closed-source baselines on several dimensions, while still exhibiting notable behaviors that warrant continued attention. Building on our findings, we highlight three key observations and recommendations. First, because safety can shift and even regress across minor updates, developers should integrate safety evaluation into incremental releases. Second, as final-turn outputs and end-state checks alone cannot reliably detect loss-of-control behaviors, deployments require process-level observability across both reasoning traces and action logs. Third, because public benchmarks elicit strong evaluation awareness and face data contamination risks, developing private benchmarks is essential for trustworthy frontier evaluation.

items.title: A Unified Arena for LLM Agents across Diverse Eurogame
items.summary: Interactive environments offer a practical way to evaluate large language model (LLM) agents, and competitive games extend this evaluation to decisions shaped by competing goals and other agents' choices. Yet existing evaluations confined to individual games or execution frameworks leave unclear which competitive advantages persist across settings. We introduce DECE (Diverse Eurogame Competitive Environments), a unified arena spanning ten Eurogames with shared interfaces and evaluation protocols. These games combine lasting strategic commitments, competition over shared resources, and multiple routes to victory. Our primary study evaluates 12 model-harness configurations, spanning nine models and four execution harnesses, in 480 three-player matches across ten games. The main and supplementary studies comprise 1,032 completed matches in total. These comparisons reveal broad cross-game ranking agreement alongside game-specific strengths. Matched studies show that the same model can perform differently across execution harnesses, adding another source of variation to these profiles. These performance advantages do not consistently translate into better token or cost efficiency, making resource use an additional consideration when comparing configurations. Together, the findings support evaluating complete agent configurations by both their competitive performance across games and the resources needed to achieve it.

items.title: From Self-Confidence to Statistical Accuracy: Scaling Human-in-the-Loop Evaluation with Direct and LLM-Assisted Auditing
items.summary:
For large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs), model-reported self-confidence is often miscalibrated, yet it may still be useful for efficient evaluation. At the same time, LLM-as-a-judge offers a scalable alternative to direct human auditing, but its practical benefit depends on calibration quality and inference cost.
  This paper develops a unified statistical framework for both evaluation routes under alternative sampling strategies. For direct auditing, confidence-stratified sampling is used to recover population accuracy from partially verified outputs without requiring calibrated confidence. Finite-sample uncertainty is characterized, and the analysis shows how highly uneven confidence strata affect audit efficiency and label allocation. For judge-assisted evaluation, the judge is modeled through sensitivity and false-positive rate, yielding an error-corrected estimator with calibration uncertainty. The two routes are then compared through human-label and total-cost efficiency boundaries.
  Experiments on MMLU-Pro and MMMU-Pro show that miscalibrated self-confidence can still support statistically valid stratified auditing. Under highly imbalanced confidence distributions, proportional allocation substantially reduces estimation error relative to equal-per-stratum allocation. For judge-assisted evaluation, only a small subset of target--verifier pairs satisfies the idealized human-label efficiency condition, and automated inference costs can further limit potential savings. These findings clarify the statistical and economic conditions under which confidence-guided auditing and automated verification are useful.

items.title: Build more responsive apps with the Decisions API
items.summary: Fast, focused, low-cost decisions for any application.
items.story_key: story|title:build more responsive apps with the decisions api
items.content_excerpt: Applications and agents make many small decisions throughout a workflow: how to classify an input, where to route a request, or which action to take next. Individually, they are simple. At scale, their latency and cost add up. Today, we’re making the Decisions API generally available. Built with GPT‑6 Luna , the Decisions API focuses Luna’s intelligence on questions with bounded answers, helping applications and agents make near real-time decisions from text, images, and structured inputs up to 10x faster than GPT‑6 Luna through the Responses API. Since public beta, we’ve added a native GPT‑Live integration, prompt caching for reused context, and inference residency in the US and EU. Developers can also pass native JSON inputs, include images in question instructions, and ask up to 400 questions per request, twice the previous limit. We’ve also continued to improve latency, including additional capacity in several regions in Asia. Early adoption of Decisions has shown its applicability across a variety of use cases. Across OpenAI, teams are applying the Decisions API across product and business workflows. The dots team is using it to reduce response times and improve interactivity. Our Personal Finance team is using it to categorize transaction descriptions, while our Communications team is using Decisions to classify coverage by the themes and scores whether it reinforces or challenges key narratives—helping identify what warrants closer review. These early examples show how fast, structured decision-making can turn incoming information into useful action across a wide range of use cases. Customers are applying the Decisions API just as broadly, from accurately attributing AI costs to making language-learning experiences more interactive. Using the Decisions API is simple: developers define a question and its allowed answers, then provide context as text, images, or native JSON. The API returns one of three supported answer types—a probability, choice, or score—that applications can use to determine what happens next. The variety of answer types allows Decisions to be applicable across a wide variety of use cases. Decisions API supports three answer types: Estimate the probability that a condition is true, such as whether a product has visible damage. Select one of your predefined options, such as whether an agent should continue, retry, or ask for clarification. choice : one of your supplied values. items.title: OpenAI models are coming to Google Cloud
items.summary: OpenAI and Google Cloud are bringing frontier models and Codex workflows to Gemini’s Model Garden, available through Google Cloud Marketplace.
items.story_key: story|title:openai models are coming to google cloud
items.content_excerpt: OpenAI and Google Cloud ⁠ (opens in a new window) are partnering to bring OpenAI’s frontier models and Codex ⁠ (opens in a new window) agentic workflows into Google Cloud’s Model Garden. The integration will give customers native access to these models to power complex agentic workflows at scale, backed by Google Cloud’s data governance and high-performance infrastructure. Google Cloud’s longstanding investment in machine learning and AI has made it a destination for AI workloads and the developers and data scientists building them. Bringing OpenAI models to its model garden gives these teams access to OpenAI’s frontier models within the environment where they already work, enabling enterprises to modernize their software development lifecycle, build agentic workflows, and change how people work. For organizations in regulated industries, deploying AI requires control over who can access sensitive data and how it is used. The integration will pair OpenAI’s frontier models with Google Cloud’s built-in access controls, centralized data governance, and high-performance infrastructure to support demanding enterprise workloads. Google Cloud customers will be able to purchase OpenAI frontier models via model garden, transacted through the Google Cloud Marketplace. Enterprises with Google Cloud spend commitments will be able to draw down their GCP commitments for these purchases. Additionally, OpenAI models will soon be available in Google Antigravity and the Gemini Agent, providing enterprise customers with model choice flexibility and the best model for each task. By expanding access through Google Cloud, we are giving enterprises greater choice in how they discover and use frontier models, with a path from evaluation to broader adoption. General availability is planned in the coming weeks. Request access to OpenAI on Google Cloud here .

items.title: Same Story, Different Lens: A Multi-Agent System for Cross-Outlet News Framing Analysis
items.summary: News outlets covering the same event differ in what they emphasize and omit. \textit{Same Story, Different Lens} is an experimental research prototype for comparing these choices. It collects world and politics coverage from 17 outlets, groups reports about the same event, and produces structured analyses of sentiment, political lean, framing, loaded language, possible omissions, and model-estimated proportions of factual claims and opinion. Loaded-language entries include quotations and neutral rewordings. Three model roles (agents) handle article analysis, assessment of source support, and cross-outlet briefing generation. Analyses are stored in a JSONL archive. The evaluation compares outlet-level lean estimates with approximate, predefined reference ratings and summarizes the Critic's model-assigned grounding scores. These measures provide preliminary diagnostics. A grounding score reflects the model's assessment of support in the supplied text and does not establish factual accuracy or constitute independent verification.

items.title: VaLoP: Value Gradient Lookahead and Pullback for Reward-Guided Diffusion
items.summary: Reward guidance steers a pretrained diffusion or flow model toward images or actions that a reward model prefers, at sampling time and without retraining the model for each reward. It follows the gradient of a value function, the expected reward given the noisy state. The two common estimates of this gradient, gradients through a one-step denoised estimate and learned value models, are least accurate at high noise, where the coarse structure of the sample is decided. Interestingly, we find that both errors are posterior covariances, which grow with the uncertainty about the clean sample, and hence at higher noise. To reduce them, we evaluate the value at a less noisy state, one sampler step ahead, where this uncertainty is smaller, and pull its gradient back to the current state. This lookahead places both estimators at the two ends of one family and reveals that an intermediate lookahead requires one additional term, a correction through the generator. We therefore propose Value Gradient Lookahead and Pullback (VaLoP), which computes this correction with one vector-Jacobian product, and VaLoP-Fast, which amortizes it with a small head that, for text-to-image models, is trained with a single reward and reused for the others. Across various models, rewards, and benchmark datasets, both robustly outperform existing value-gradient guidance on the target reward, VaLoP-Fast at about the cost of learned-value guidance. Both extend to critic-guided robot policies, where VaLoP-Fast attains the highest success rates on LIBERO and RoboCasa.

items.title: Serving DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at Scale: vLLM Matches DeepInfer and Scales to GB300 NVL72
items.summary: With P/D disaggregation and Wide-EP on a GB300 NVL72 rack, vLLM serves DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on SemiAnalysis AgentX at 954K tokens/s per GPU at a P90 of 196 tokens/s per user, 7.9x our aggregated single-node result.
items.story_key: model:deepseek|ver:4.1|variant:flash|title:serving deepseek v4 1 flash at scale vllm matches deepinfer and scales to gb300
items.content_excerpt: TL;DR: On one NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 rack, vLLM with P/D disaggregation and Wide-EP serves DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on SemiAnalysis AgentX at 954K tokens/s per GPU at a P90 of 196 tokens/s per user, 7.9× our single-node result from the first post and $38.96 per GPU-hour at DeepSeek's off-peak prices. A specialized decode path reaches 826 tokens/s for a single user. Against DeepInfer, DeepSeek's own engine, vLLM's decode throughput is within 6% across batch sizes 8–256, and its prefill tracks DeepInfer's published curve. The efficiency comes from deliberate engineering on components that vLLM already has, built on the kernels DeepSeek open-sourced. This post walks through our performance study, breaks down each optimization, and shares the lessons we learned: Figure 1: SemiAnalysis AgentX on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72: vLLM with P/D disaggregation and Wide-EP (gold) achieves a further 7.9× throughput increase over our aggregated single-node result from the first post . Throughput counts cached input, uncached input and output tokens ( source ). DeepInfer is DeepSeek's own inference engine for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, released this week as an offline engine with published prefill and decode curves. It is the most relevant reference for this model, so before going into our optimizations we show where vLLM stands against it. Decode. Under DeepSeek's decode configuration (131K context, nextn=3), vLLM on GB200 achieves throughput within 6% of DeepInfer's published results across batch sizes 8 to 256 (Figure 2). Figure 2: Decode output throughput per GPU vs. batch size at 131K context, nextn=3. vLLM on GB200 vs. DeepInfer's published results, read from the charts in its README ( source ). Prefill. DeepInfer's published prefill curve uses EP4DP4 with 32 redundant experts and a 140-token bounded replay, on hardware the chart does not state, and we read its values off the chart. Our run uses DEP2 on GB300 with no redundant experts, a 128-token replay and our own prompts. Because the setups differ, we do not read the gap between the two curves as an engine-to-engine speedup. What Figure 3 shows is that vLLM's DEP2 prefill tracks DeepSeek's own engine across the range they published. Figure 3: Prefill throughput vs. new tokens. vLLM DEP2 on GB300 vs. DeepInfer's published curve (EP4DP4, 32 redundant experts, 140-token replay, hardware not stated), read from the chart in its README ( source ). items.title: claude-code v2.1.310
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added the Monitor tool and plugin monitors on Bedrock, Vertex, and Foundry, and when telemetry or nonessential traffic is disabled; long foreground sleeps are now blocked there too
  • Fixed requests failing behind some gateways and compatible servers that reject the effort-2025-11-24 beta value or mid-conversation system messages; Claude Code now retries without them
  • Fixed background cleanup deleting some recent files, such as pasted images, when cleanupPeriodDays is set to a very large value
  • Fixed compaction after a "Prompt is too long" error keeping too much of a conversation with dense text, such as base64 or SVG, so the next request could fail again
  • Fixed file read permission prompts not showing where a symbolic link leads
  • Fixed a question's auto-continue timeout firing the moment the external editor closed after a long edit
  • Windows: Fixed PreToolUse and PermissionRequest hooks letting a tool call through when Git Bash is missing and the hook's command is only quoted strings, such as a quoted path
  • Improved auto mode's prompt before the first read outside the working directories: it now says when blocking those reads makes shell commands ask for permission
  • Improved memory use of non-interactive sessions (-p, Agent SDK) during compaction when the transcript file is very large
  • Improved a mod's Image to draw inside tmux with allow-passthrough and focus-events on, in kitty, Ghostty, and iTerm2 3.5+ with fullscreen rendering, where it showed only its alt text
  • Linux: Improved /sandbox and the sandbox startup warning to name Ubuntu's AppArmor restriction on user namespaces, and how to lift it, when it keeps bubblewrap from starting the sandbox
  • Changed the error for an MCP tool call that times out in a non-interactive session while the server's elicitation is unanswered: it now tells Claude that no answer came and not to repeat the call
  • [VSCode] Fixed pressing Enter on the plan review card's "Send feedback and keep planning" button approving the plan instead of sending your comments back
  • [VSCode] Fixed the panel showing "Something went wrong" after "Switch branch & continue" on a cloud session opened from Session history's Web tab
  • [Cloud sessions] Added Claude Code cloud sessions and Remote Control permissions to Enterprise custom roles, so Owners can control access to each by role
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a Choose file button to load a cloud environment's setup script from a file
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed failed saves and archives in the cloud environment edit dialog showing no error inside the dialog
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed failed routine API token actions showing only a toast; the error now appears in the routine edit dialog
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved the session start checklist to show a cloud environment's setup script output in a scrolling box
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed turning on Cloud sessions or Remote Control in admin settings to ask for confirmation and list the custom roles that have that permission
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed the cloud environment dialog to open network access, setup script and environment variables from rows instead of listing every editor at once
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag treating ! commands such as !restart and !help as ordinary messages when sent in bold, italic or strikethrough
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag admin channel and workspace pages being replaced by a load error when a background refresh of the bundle list fails
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag's spend limits page in admin settings reporting that no channels match a filter while channel names are still loading
  • [Code Review] Fixed the Code Review admin section hiding its repositories and switches after a failed refresh of the repository list
  • [Code Review] Improved the Code Review admin section to retry the first load and show one Try again banner when it still fails
